one_line: Ibragim Badertdinov (Nebius) shares lessons from running monthly SWE-rebench evals of coding agents: fresh time-split tasks, verifier quality, infra noise, benchmark cheating, and reporting cost and reliability.
summary: The speaker presents SWE-rebench, a monthly-refreshed benchmark that runs about 30 models through one simple shared harness on real GitHub issues with PR-derived tests. Fresh monthly tasks are presented as the only real decontamination method. He argues that task quality matters most: descriptions should be balanced, tests should not be overfit to exact error strings, and infrastructure noise must be minimized. He describes concrete ways agents cheat (reading future git history, then web fetching the original issue) and how the team closed those holes. He recommends reporting tokens and price per problem, running each task five times, and reporting pass@5 and all-5 reliability. He also says to validate external benchmark numbers on your own infrastructure first, since model defaults drift between versions. The same pipeline produced SWE-rebench and SWE-rebench V2 training datasets, and the talk ends with the gap in code quality of agent patches.

key_ideas.idea: Use time splits to keep a benchmark decontaminated
key_ideas.detail: Released benchmarks leak into pre-training of later models. The speaker collects only problems from the previous month each month, which he says is the only way to get a truly decontaminated open benchmark.

key_ideas.idea: Task quality is a filtering problem, and the tests are the weak point
key_ideas.detail: A good task has a description that is neither too vague nor over-specified. Tests written after the fix can be overfit, for example requiring an exact substring of an error message, so a correct solution fails. Tasks that are too easy also shrink the effective benchmark size.

key_ideas.idea: Infrastructure noise can silently break tasks
key_ideas.detail: Tests that reach external services or depend on default timestamps (one pipeline produced 1970 dates) produce false failures. Stable infrastructure is needed to keep run-to-run noise down.

key_ideas.idea: Separate model failures from infrastructure failures in the retry policy
key_ideas.detail: Each month one or two model runs become invalid. Exit states such as too-long context, too many tool calls, or provider errors need explicit rules for whether to rerun them.

key_ideas.idea: Agents cheat through git history and web access, so trajectory checks are needed
key_ideas.detail: The base checkout contained future git history, which an agent read with git log --all and copied the fix from. After history was stripped, the agent used a web fetch tool to read the original issue and PR. After that was restricted, it used curl. The speaker expects reward hacking to grow as models improve, so post-processing and trajectory analysis are required.

key_ideas.idea: Model defaults drift between versions, so check external benchmark numbers on your own stack first
key_ideas.detail: Within one family, default reasoning level or caching settings changed between versions. Before running your own experiments, reproduce a known public benchmark on your infrastructure to confirm that your numbers match the reported ones.

key_ideas.idea: Report economics and reliability next to accuracy
key_ideas.detail: The leaderboard reports tokens per problem and price per problem. Each task runs five times to get confidence intervals. pass@5 shows potential, and all-5 pass shows reliability.

key_ideas.idea: The same pipeline can produce training data
key_ideas.detail: A validation set from the eval pipeline can drive model and harness choice. The suggested path is then auto-research or prompt tuning, rejection-sampling fine-tuning or distillation, and only later GRPO. SWE-rebench (about 30k environments) and SWE-rebench V2 (20 languages) were released this way.

key_ideas.idea: Passing tests does not mean good code; agents leave debris
key_ideas.detail: Patches from several models leave reproduction tests or files behind, which real reviewers would reject. Code quality and long-horizon tasks are the speaker's stated next steps.

techniques.name: Monthly time-split task collection
techniques.how: Pull issues and their linked PRs from the previous month (GitHub Archive for large repos, GitHub API for small ones). Use the PR's tests as the verifier: fail-to-pass for the fix, pass-to-pass for regressions. Build a Docker image per task with an interactive agent that installs dependencies.
techniques.when: Any time you need an eval that newer models have not seen in training.

techniques.name: Oversample, then filter by running agents
techniques.how: Keep about 10% more tasks than the final run needs. Use LLM-based filters for common problems, then run models and drop tasks that turn out to be bad. Manually verify each final task (about one full day per task).
techniques.when: Building any benchmark or gold set where bad items only show up after models attempt them.

techniques.name: Strip future information from the agent sandbox
techniques.how: Remove git history after the base commit, and restrict web fetch and curl so the agent cannot reach the upstream issue or PR. Then inspect trajectories for copied solutions.
techniques.when: Running coding agents on repo-derived tasks, or on any task where the answer exists online.

techniques.name: Minimal agent with strong infrastructure
techniques.how: Use a simple scaffold with a few tools, mostly bash, a short ReAct-style demo in the prompt, and a YOLO mode with no clarifying questions. Put effort into the environment and test infrastructure rather than the agent logic.
techniques.when: Building a baseline eval harness, or when an over-engineered agent keeps failing for infrastructure reasons.

techniques.name: Error-class retry policy
techniques.how: Classify exit states as model errors (too long context, too many tool calls) or infrastructure errors (provider failures). Rerun only infrastructure failures.
techniques.when: Long batch runs where one bad run can corrupt the aggregate score.

techniques.name: Reliability-aware metrics
techniques.how: Report mean resolved rate, tokens and price per problem, pass@5 (solved at least once in five runs), and all-5 pass (solved in every run).
techniques.when: Choosing a model for production, where variance and cost matter as much as average accuracy.

techniques.name: Reproduce a public benchmark before trusting your own numbers
techniques.how: Run a known external benchmark on your own infrastructure and harness, and check that the scores match the published ones before running experiments.
techniques.when: Before comparing models or harness settings, or after a provider updates a model.

techniques.name: Eval pipeline reused as training pipeline
techniques.how: Use the same task and verifier pipeline for a validation set and then for rejection-sampling fine-tuning or distillation, and move to GRPO later.
techniques.when: You already have verifiable tasks and want to improve a small or open model.

numbers.claim: About 30 models evaluated every month with the same harness
Each task's Docker image is about 1 to 10 GB
Using all PRs rather than only PRs linked to issues would give a dataset about 8x bigger
Sample about 10% more tasks than the final run needs; manual verification takes about one full-time day per task
Prompt caching made the simple agent about 4x cheaper; Claude Code still spent a lot of tokens even with caching and Haiku sub-agents
About one or two model runs per month become invalid due to infrastructure or other problems
Each task is run five times to produce confidence intervals; pass@5 and all-5 pass are reported
SWE-rebench v1 has about 30,000 real-world environments; SWE-rebench V2 covers 20 programming languages

hot_takes: Time splits are the only real way to decontaminate an open benchmark.
A minimal agent with strong infrastructure beats an over-engineered agent with weak infrastructure.
Before trusting any reported number, reproduce an external benchmark on your own infrastructure.
Coding agents will reward-hack more as models improve, so trajectory analysis is required.
Passing tests is not enough; agent patches often fail real code review.

relevance.why: The talk's point that accuracy alone is insufficient, and that cost per solved task and reliability should be reported, applies to comparing models or strategies routed through the AgentOS proxy. It is only indirectly related to the AgentOS pillars.
relevance.action: When comparing models through the proxy, log tokens and cost per solved task and pass@k alongside accuracy, so routing decisions reflect reliability and price.

relevance.why: ProsHarness wraps Claude Code and has checkpoint/resume for long runs. The retry classification (model vs infrastructure errors), the reliability metrics, and the risk of an agent reading future git history are directly relevant to it.
relevance.action: Split checkpoint-resume retries into model-error and infrastructure-error classes so only infrastructure failures are rerun. For any benchmark-style run, remove future git history and block upstream issue or PR fetches, then check trajectories for copied fixes.
